# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, solution, then sending, which suits me, but the look-back window (screen 4) splits the context screen into two halves (3 and 5) that carry the same heading and prompt, so the context step feels interrupted rather than finished in one place.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 repeat the same prompt ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'). Screen 2 ('Where are the people who would buy this?') also overlaps the context's 'where: US', which I would expect screens 3 or 5 to confirm again. Screens 12 and 13 show the Compatibility check twice, the second after the review.
founder.missing: Nothing asks who pays or what it costs. My buyer is the cluster operator or department head, not the researcher who submits the job, and I price per cluster a month (I would test $10,000 to $20,000). Nothing captures the existing cost they would weigh that against, which is the 30% to 59% of reserved GPU hours that sit idle. Nothing asks what stands in the way of buying, chiefly a security review of an agent installed on every node. Screen 20 ('Offer a pilot?') covers the free two-week measurement but not the price or the buyer behind the paid pilot.

PRIMARY.order_why: The question about whether I ran my own source code is a qualifying question about my last job, but it comes after the idea card in Part 2 instead of with the other questions about my recent work in Part 1.
PRIMARY.missing: Why the job was killed (out of memory, hit the time limit, or a GPU fault), how I currently decide what memory, GPUs and run time to request, and how much work or time I lost when it died.

screens.why4: The one chip, I'm not sure, is the right escape for a founder who can't name the conditions, and the box takes my three lines as I wrote them.
screens.why5: My three lines (the monitoring agent on the node, their own source code rather than a licensed binary, and Python) stand exactly as I typed them.
screens.why7: Three verb-phrase rows under 16 words fit the shape, but 'could run a monitoring agent on the job's node' is really the cluster operator's permission typed as the researcher's ability, so the review will have to rewrite it to say who allows it.
screens.instead: How does it fit into what they already do today? e.g. 'kept the job's source code on the cluster' or 'was allowed to have an agent running on their job's node'

screens.why1: After I typed how it fits what researchers already do, checking the conditions Keel drew from that answer is the obvious next step before I pick one to test.
screens.why2: Monitoring agent, node, licensed program and Python are everyday words on a SLURM or Kubernetes cluster, and each row reads whole after 'Most researchers who run jobs on shared GPU clusters'.
screens.why3: Source code and Python are things a researcher knows about their own job, but whether an agent can run on the node is the cluster operator's call, so a researcher would guess at it.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct and cover my mechanism, but 'Wrote the job's code in Python' fails the researcher who ran a colleague's copied Python script, when what matters is whether the code was Python.
screens.why5: These are my own conditions: an agent on every node, reading the source code rather than a licensed binary, and the profiler being Python-only for now.
screens.why7: The agent row opens on 'could' as an ability, but whether an agent runs on the node is a permission the operator holds, so a researcher's 'Yes, easily' or 'Only sometimes' has no true footing; the review should have rewritten it as 'was allowed to have a monitoring agent on the job's node'.
screens.instead: Keep the rows but reword two: 'Was allowed to have a monitoring agent on the job's node' (permission) and 'Ran code written in Python' (fact).

screens.why1: Right after my Save of the Compatibility Check, showing what the review changed before I pick the one to test is exactly where this belongs, and I pressed Continue without needing anything else.
screens.why2: Monitoring agent, the job's node, source code versus a licensed program, Python: these are my trade's plain words and I read all three rows at once.
screens.why3: These are the three things I know my product leans on (the node agent, reading the code, the Python-only profiler), so I can judge them from what I know of my users' clusters.
screens.why4: Three distinct rows, inside the 2-to-4 band, each one thing, none overlapping and none filler.
screens.why5: The review turned my 'could run a monitoring agent' into 'were allowed to run' one, which rightly makes it a permission, but in my product the operator installs the agent on every node and the researcher never runs it, so the act has drifted onto the wrong person.
screens.why7: The source-code and Python rows are clean facts, and the agent row is correctly a permission with no settled SLURM/K8s row left, but 'Wrote the job's code in Python' is narrower than the mechanism (only the line-level profiler is Python-only, while the size prediction is not), so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Had a monitoring agent installed on the job's node by the cluster's operators · Ran their own source code, not a licensed program · Could change the job's code to apply a suggested fix

screens.why1: Right after I checked and reviewed my conditions, picking the one to put to strangers is the obvious next step, and the intro says why only one goes out.
screens.why2: Monitoring agent, the job's node, source code, licensed program and Python are everyday words on a SLURM cluster, and each row reads cleanly after 'Most researchers'.
screens.why3: I know which of my conditions breaks most often in the field (the licensed binaries like VASP or Gaussian), so I can pick from what I know of my users.
screens.why4: Three distinct conditions, all mine as reviewed: the agent permission, own code versus a licensed binary, and Python for the profiler; none overlaps and none is a settled SLURM-or-K8s row.
screens.why5: My pick, 'ran their own source code, not a licensed program', is carried word for word into the belief and the test, and nothing is reworded here as promised.
screens.why7: The picked fact is right for the card: true for some and false for others, testable either way, with the fact's bar 'no more than 1 in 3 say no'; but the box shown before the pick quotes the permission bar ('only with help or approval, or no'), which never applies to a fact, so the bar shifts between the empty box and the filled one.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but before the pick have the box say 'Holds if no more than 1 in 3 answer against' so it fits whichever row I pick; then after picking the own-code row show 'Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say no'.

screens.why1: Right after I said how Expanse fits the scheduler and the code, it is obvious to ask what it does better than padding and guessing, before strangers are asked whether it would have helped.
screens.why2: Plain to me: one benefit a line, up to four, nine words each, and "what researchers would get that today's way does not give them" is exactly how I would put it, though the example ("less time on it each week") is generic rather than cluster-shaped.
screens.why3: I know what Expanse gives a researcher over over-requesting: the job runs to the end first time, and a smaller request waits less in the queue.
screens.why4: The only option is the *I'm not sure* chip, which is the card's founder-side escape and fits a box I may not be able to fill.
screens.why5: The two benefits I typed ("A job that runs to the end first time; A shorter wait in the queue") stand as I wrote them, one a line, nothing reworded on this screen.
screens.why7: The box asks what the card requires: 1 to 4 benefits, each up to 9 words, each naming what changes against today's way, with *I'm not sure* as the founder's escape; my two rows are distinct noun phrases, the one I lead with first, no number I didn't write.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Expanse does better than today's way, Keel shows back the benefits it drafted and what it will test, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Both rows are in my words, but the belief reads awkwardly on first pass: 'their last job that failed mid-run would have given them a job that runs to the end first time' makes a job give a job, and I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether a job dies mid-run and how long it sits in the queue are things every researcher on a shared SLURM or K8s cluster lives with on every submission.
screens.why4: Two distinct benefits, no overlap, each well under 9 words, in plain cluster language, with the 1-to-4 guidance and room to add or remove.
screens.why5: These are the two I gave, the job running first time ('debug failures in seconds, not days') and a smaller request fitting sooner, kept in my order with nothing added.
screens.why7: The rows are noun phrases of what changes against today's padding and guessing, my lead benefit is first, both are joined with 'and' in the belief on the study's hurt (the job that failed mid-run, not any last job), and the bar counts 'no difference' and 'worse' against, so the belief can be refuted.
screens.instead: Keep both rows; word the belief as: For most, with it, their last job that failed mid-run would have run to the end first time, with a shorter wait in the queue.

screens.why1: After fit and advantage, asking what effort it takes researchers to start using it is the obvious next question in the solution step.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps and learning are plain to a researcher submitting jobs, and the hint's limits of four rows and 9 words are clear.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my researchers would have to change: trust the predicted sizes instead of padding, and apply the code fixes we surface.
screens.why4: The only chip is I'm not sure, which fits a founder who cannot name the effort and leaves the dimension out as the card says.
screens.why5: My two efforts went in as I typed them, and nothing of mine is reworded on this screen.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 short steps researchers take themselves, and my two rows are each one such step with no sign-off and no Compatibility or Purchase friction overlap; their voice is set on the next screen.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start using it, Keel shows the efforts back for me to check before I pick one to test, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Padding a request and line-level fixes are how researchers on SLURM clusters talk, so both rows read first time, though the intro repeats the title 'What they'll have to do' word for word.
screens.why3: Both efforts are the researcher's own at submit time: whether to trust the predicted memory, GPUs and walltime over their usual margin, and whether to edit their own code.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one a habit at submit and one a change to the code, both in my words, with nothing missing that a researcher does themselves (the agent install is the operator's).
screens.why5: These are my two adoption frictions as I wrote them from the launch: use the sizes instead of over-requesting, and apply the line-level optimisations.
screens.why7: Each row is one effort the researcher takes themselves, a base-form verb phrase under 9 words in one voice, none of them Compatibility's or Purchase friction's ground, two of the allowed 1 to 4, and the first is the habit first use asks, so a yes or a no can answer the belief.

screens.why1: Right after I checked my own list of start-up efforts, picking the one most likely to stop a researcher is the obvious next step before the stranger's question is built.
screens.why2: Both rows are in my trade's own words: 'padding' a request and 'line-level code fixes' are what researchers and ML engineers on a SLURM or K8s cluster already say.
screens.why3: Whether to trust a predicted size over your own padded guess, and whether to apply a suggested code change, are things every researcher decides themselves at each submit.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct efforts, both mine, neither bundling two steps, and the one I'd pick (dropping the padding) is there, which is the real catch since everyone over-requests two to three times.
screens.why5: The rows are mine as typed, which the screen says it does not reword, and the belief 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding' is exactly the bet I make when I say our models over-provision rather than under-provision.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form efforts the researcher takes themselves, with no sign-off, no setup by my team and no overlap with Compatibility or Purchase friction; the picked row gives a belief that Yes and Only-if can support and Probably not and No can refute, with the bar at 1 in 3 and the escape left to the stranger's item.

screens.why1: Last step before strangers see the study, so deciding whether to collect leads belongs here, and we are onboarding paid pilots and want every cluster that will talk to us.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with the exact line respondents will see in the hint is plain on first reading.
screens.why3: Whether I want names of people ready to try Expanse is my own call; it is the HN post's 'we'd love to have a talk' ask.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it; the two options are distinct, plain and complete for a single switch.
screens.why5: Yes keeps my intent, but the generic 'Would you try this for real?' drifts from my actual offer: a free two-week waste measurement on the cluster, which only an operator can say yes to, not a researcher submitting jobs.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Yes, ask them / No pilot, with the end line in my words: "Would you let Expanse measure your cluster's waste free for two weeks? Leave your email."

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the researchers the questions belongs in the last step before the link goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, voice, typing, credits and text messages into one paragraph, and says 'records the voice' while the interviewer is on video with a face, so I'd read it twice to know what I'm locking.
screens.why3: Picking the voice my researchers will hear is my call, and the 5-second previews let me judge it myself.
screens.why4: Two distinct interviewers, each with a preview and a default already picked, and no escape chip needed for a choice between two voices.
screens.why5: It addresses 'researchers' as I typed them and leaks nothing of Expanse's product or the operator role to the respondent side.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions? (Each interviewer appears on video and speaks every question, which is also written on screen; your pick is recorded once for this project, 400 credits either way.) Daphne ▶ 5 s / Saskia ▶ 5 s

screens.why1: Right before sending, choosing how researchers will answer is the natural last decision, and it follows the interviewer screen.
screens.why2: Video interviewer versus read-and-tap is plain to me, and each option says what the researcher actually does.
screens.why3: I know my researchers sit at terminals and would rather read and tap than talk to a video, so I can answer from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three ways are complete and distinct (voice-and-video, text, or their choice), and no escape is needed for a founder's setting.
screens.why5: It names my people as I typed them, researchers and ML engineers, and leaks nothing of the product to them.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how researchers answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending, and I'd want to reach researchers I know at the HPC centres and labs by name.
screens.why2: Three plain choices; the only odd bits are "the Contacts page" and the Google sign-in, and they explain themselves well enough.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to named researchers from our pilot conversations and the HN thread or posting in a Slack or mailing list, so this is mine to answer.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list, and one open link for a group cover the real ways I'd reach researchers, they're distinct, and no escape is needed for a routing choice.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is touched here; it is pure sending logistics and my pick, people I know by name, is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title with '4 counted' beside it, and each card right below says '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know why it is not called.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on the stage page, but the kicker and the cards make it plain: 7 answered, 4 counted on each belief, and the bar is 5, though I would like to know why 3 of the 7 were not counted.
screens.why_b3: The beliefs are recognisably mine, but the statement under the title is garbled ('the researcher or ML engineer on every node' where the agent should be, and the 'actually needs' clause doubled), and the Relative advantage line reads clumsily with 'their last job that failed mid-run would have given them a job that runs'.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' hints that I need one more counted answer on each belief, but the page never says to send the study to more researchers or how many more.
screens.why_b5: Nothing is claimed beyond 4 counted of 7; it calls every belief too few to call rather than leaning either way.
screens.instead: Too few to call: each belief has 4 of 7 counted and needs 5, so send it to a few more researchers on 100+ GPU clusters. Fix my solution line so the agent, not the researcher, sits on every node.

screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "ran their own source code, not a licensed program" are the condition I picked, in my words, over my researchers and ML engineers; only the bar line's clipped "You said ran ..." and the doubled "Asked: Asked:" read rough.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic: it does not tell me that one more counted answer would decide it, or that every counted answer so far leans my way.
screens.why_b5: It says it is a small group, a lean and not a call, keeps 5 answered and 4 counted visible, says why Rafael was dropped, and claims nothing beyond the four.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted with 5 needed, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts 3 better against 1 same over 4 people, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' mixes the five-person floor with the one-in-three rule, so I need a second look to see where my bar sits.
screens.why_b3: The belief line carries both benefits I typed, running first time and a shorter queue wait, under the dimension name I checked, though the bar line repeats only the first.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not tell me that one more counted answer would decide it, or that Kwabena's no difference comes from someone whose sizes already work.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both, so they agree.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count answers per option over 5 answered and 4 counted, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5', with its marker at 4, reads like a for-count I've already met rather than the 1-in-3-against bar or the floor of 5, so the bar needs a second look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would use the suggested sizes instead of padding' are the effort I picked in my own words, though the 'You said use the suggested sizes…' bar line is clumsily worded.

screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more answer, but the screen doesn't say so, and it doesn't say what Kwabena's 'no difference' means for the pitch to researchers whose sizes already come from past runs.

screens.why_b6: Kwabena's line teaches me something I didn't type: for someone already sizing from last week's runs, the day goes to data staging and library conflicts, not job sizing, so first-time runs aren't the pain for that user.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it obviously checks whether I am in the study's segment of researchers on large shared GPU clusters.
screens.why2: Cluster, GPUs and jobs are everyday words in my work, and I can answer it at a glance.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our shared cluster is, but someone who uses a slice of a big cloud or a partition of a national system might have to guess whether it counts as 100 or more.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a gate takes no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of clusters of 100 or more GPUs and leaks nothing of a product.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and the yes or no is easy to hold when heard.
screens.instead: Do the jobs you submit run on a shared cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes or No.

screens.why1: Right after the cluster screener, asking whether a job of mine got killed this week is the obvious next step before asking for the story.
screens.why2: 'Job killed before it finished' is how we talk on SLURM; I'd answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly which of my jobs died this week, because I check sacct and my logs every morning.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the two chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is a job killed because I under-asked for memory, GPUs or wall time, but 'killed' alone also takes in preemption, node failures and my own scancel, so the reason that made it a problem has dropped out.
screens.why6: One short sentence, then 'Yes or no', is easy to hold and answer by ear.
screens.why7: It is on the gate's two fixed answers with no escape, it asks the costly event rather than the routine, and a No-sayer exists (all my jobs ran to the end), but dropping 'hit its memory or time limit' bends the one-clause rule, so preempted or crashed jobs count as Yes.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job of yours get killed for running past its memory or time limit? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said a job of mine got killed this week, it makes sense to show me an idea about guessing a job's needs before I submit it.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, walltime, GPU memory, submission script and node are all everyday words in my work, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: It's about the exact thing I do every time I submit: guess memory, GPUs and time and hope the job isn't killed.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It's shown on purpose as an idea, in words a cluster user would use, and the belief stays on telling me what each job needs at submit time.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, the middle runs to four sentences and a feature list, and 'GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime' stumbles on 'memory' twice, so it's more than I'd hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, software that predicts each job's needs when you submit it. It reads your code, script and hardware, then tells you the GPU memory, RAM, CPUs and walltime to ask for, and warns you before a job would fail. The people building it believe it would tell you what each job actually needs at submit time.

screens.why1: After the Expanse card I can guess they want to know if my job could be read or profiled, but jumping to whose code I ran feels abrupt and its link to predicting needs at submit time isn't obvious.
screens.why2: 'Your own source code' is plain to me, but 'licensed program' isn't how we talk: the PyTorch and Hugging Face stack I run is open source and technically licensed, so I'd have to stop and work out what they mean.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my last job was, my own fine-tuning script, so I can answer from what I did.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' makes no sense for whose code it was, and there's no clean answer for my own script running on top of open-source libraries.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks past the card, but 'own source code, not a licensed program' reads like someone else's framing of the condition rather than a plain test of it.
screens.why6: Short, one question, three options I can hold, and one escape said last; the tacked-on 'not a licensed program' is the only slightly clunky bit.
screens.why7: Nearly every ML researcher on a GPU cluster runs their own training code, so everyone answers Yes and the belief can't be refuted, while the condition the pitch rests on (trusting predicted memory, GPUs and run time instead of your own over-request) goes untested.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. Could you have let a tool set its memory, GPUs and run time for you when you submitted it? Yes, easily · Yes, with some steps · Only with help or approval · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, it makes sense to ask whether this would have helped with the job I just said got killed.
screens.why2: I get 'failed mid-run' and 'each job's needs', but 'done that better' makes me stop: better at what, failing? It would read cleaner as 'saved that job' or 'kept it from dying'.
screens.why3: I lost a fine-tuning run to under-requested memory this week, so I can answer this from my own job.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it, and 'I can't tell' fits apart for a job whose cause I never pinned down.
screens.why5: It is the idea card's own line, predicting needs at submit, with no benefit or pitch smuggled into the question or the options.
screens.why6: One sentence I can follow by ear, four short options and one escape, nothing only the eye reads.
screens.why7: The four fixed answers, the order and the escape are right, but 'the last job that failed mid-run' is wider than the hurt the study screened for (killed for running out of memory or time), so a job that died from a code bug or a node fault pulls answers to 'No difference' for reasons that have nothing to do with predicting needs.
screens.instead: Think of the last job that was killed for running out of memory or time. Would Expanse, software on every node that predicts each job's needs, have saved that job for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after asking whether Expanse would have done better on my failed job, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually trust its numbers over my own padding.
screens.why2: "Padding your requests" is exactly how I'd say it, but "suggested sizes" is vague: I'd think in memory, GPUs and wall time, not "sizes", so I had to map it on a second read.
screens.why3: I pad every submission because under-requesting kills jobs mid-run, so whether I'd drop that habit is squarely my call and my life.
screens.why4: Yes, a conditional yes, probably not and no are distinct and complete, and "only if it matches what my job needs" is the real catch I'd name, with I can't tell fitting as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card itself, and the step reads as a researcher's own habit change rather than the founder's product language.
screens.why6: One short question, four short options said as a list, and the escape last, so it is easy to hold on one hearing.
screens.why7: The effort is one I take myself (trusting the suggestion instead of padding), the options are the fixed four in order with a specific own-condition rather than a fear, the belief can be supported or refuted, and I can't tell is there as the escape.
screens.instead: To use Expanse, you'd request the memory, GPUs and time it suggests instead of padding them. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it matches what my job needs · Probably not · No · I can't tell
